dhq:abstract.p: This paper considers the three phases and five decades of the Women’s Labour History Project (WLHP) archive. It documents a transmediated feminist archival process, which has its origins in the pre-digital world and makes use of various technologies, and arrives at Crossing Fonds, a digital humanities initiative. Transmediation represents the process of moving records from one medium to another in ways that conserve but also offer new opportunities. The WLHP engaged in critical archival studies from the 1970s to the 1990s, exploring human and archival memory, undertaking a forensic search for relevant bibliographic and archival records regarding women, work, and labour organization, and then growing into a multi-decade reuse of archival footage to reinterpret diverse histories. Decades later, the first phase led to Phase Two, the activation of Women’s Labour History Project series as a component of the larger Sara Diamond fonds—a collection within the Crista Dahl Media Library & Archive (CDMLA) at VIVO Media Arts through digitization and generous interfaces built to encourage access. Phase Three is Case Study 1 within the larger Crossing Fonds Omeka S archival collaboration platform. Digital archives provide the opportunity to develop new analyses prompted by access to documents from institutional and community archives. Researchers can redescribe, contextualize, and apply critical archival practices to consider new relationships, including between items and fonds.

div.head: Introduction
div.p:
This article considers the three phases and five decades of the Women’s Labour History Project (WLHP) archive. It documents a transmediated feminist archival process, which has its origins in the pre-digital world and makes use of various technologies, and arrives at Crossing Fonds, a digital humanities initiative. Transmediation draws from Peña and Kedrick’s (2023) broad definition, Whatever the nature of media, transmediation intends to account for the transference of content between different forms of it . Transmediation can include ideas, works, media itself, semiotic systems, sensory, signal and raw data. This article considers continuities and new opportunities informed by capabilities in the online archive field, maturation of critical archival studies, and changing user needs. It begins with a brief overview of the Crossing Fonds Omeka S archival collaboration platform. It then discusses the three phases of the WLHP. Phase One (1970s–1990s) – WLHP and Feminist Archival Activism engaged human and archival memory, undertaking a forensic search for relevant bibliographic and archival records regarding women, work, and labour organization and then a multi-decade reuse of archival footage to reinterpret diverse histories. Decades later, the first phase led to Phase Two – Bringing the WLHP/Diamond fonds to VIVO Media Arts, the creation of the Women’s Labour History Project fonds in 2018 as a component of the larger Sara Diamond fonds — a collection within the Crista Dahl Media Library & Archive (CDMLA) at VIVO Media Arts.
VIVO Media Arts Centre (est. 1973) located in Vancouver, Canada, is a non-profit, artist-run centre originally founded as a free public library of international alternative video . It supports experimental media practice through low-barrier access to education, exhibition, production, and distribution. Its Crista Dahl Media Library & Archive (CDMLA) is a counter-archive holding the complex histories of video and media art and the communities who created them.
CDMLA undertook extensive digitization and created a transmediated series of public facing WLHP web experiences. Phase Three – Crossing Fonds Case Study – Women’s Labour History: Restaurant Work in the Vancouver Area uses the Omeka S platform to investigate women’s labour and labour organization in British Columbia, Canada’s restaurant and hotel sectors in the 1930s, 1940s, and 1970s. Researchers sought to inform the platform’s ability to provide new pathways and relationships that are metadata-driven and that traverse diverse sources, supporting new realizations and welcoming community engagement and reinterpretation. The platform itself acts as a transmediated space beyond its singular items. This essay discusses the tools and analysis enabled by the platform and the contribution to feminist labour history and digital archival research.

figure.head: A screen capture compilation representing the Crossing Fonds Case Study 1 landing page, showing Primary item sets (left), a description of Case Study 1, and a portion of the Parent Set of individual items with titles.

div.p:
Crossing Fonds is an Omeka S digital humanities platform that supports collaborative access across institutional, community, and counter archives. It was created by Simon Fraser Archives, SFU Library and Special Collections, City of Vancouver Archives, VIVO Media Arts Centre (Crista Dahl Media Library & Archive), BC Labour Heritage Centre, OCAD University Visual Analytics Lab, The Centre for the Black Canadian Diaspora, and the Black Arts Centre (BLAC), Surrey. This coalition produced Crossing Fonds to encourage collaboration between researchers, archivists, community members, artists, and other participants. Bringing together these distinct types of archives opens the range of digital materials relevant to diverse participants and does so in a spirit of collaboration, reciprocity, co-design, and co-learning. Community and counter archives provide records that inspire alternative interpretations of histories, including those of marginalized groups, artists, and activists .
The goal is to enable scholarship, community-driven projects, and reinterpretation of collections through inclusive filters. When connected to institutional holdings, a rich discursive space is enabled that can challenge hegemonic understandings of the past. Users can collaboratively create new interpretations of historical records and illustrate connections between official documents and personal items within a shared space. Collections related to one organization or person already cross archives for pragmatic or institutional reasons (changes in status of an organization for example, or the wishes of different donors who create the records of a singular entity or even funder requirements). Linking archives and collections databases, and allowing searches across institutions, is not new. See https://www.memorybc.ca/. In Canada, several provincial archive associations maintain pan-provincial archive databases such as MemoryBC
However, designs that deploy linked data strategies across archives are rare.

The Crossing Fonds platform is an open-source digital ecosystem/platform.
https://crossingfonds.com/ provides access to the full Crossing Fonds project and the Omeka S site.
The platform is hosted on the Digital Research Alliance of Canada with a WordPress interface that provides access to the Omeka S site, information about the project, and documentation of its 2024 symposium. The Crossing Fonds Omeka S site supports multiple media formats, allowing users to display relationships between related items (individual digital objects with metadata) of different media. Crossing Fonds can manage items and metadata description from Collective Access, AtoM, and DublinCore (metadata standards). There are examples of effective Omeka S applications such as the Union of BC Indian Chiefs archive (https://www.ubcic.bc.ca/library) that served as inspiration. Crossing Fonds designers (Kahani Ploessl, OCAD U; Syr Reifsteck, VIVO) and creating resource templates based upon the Resource Data Framework (RDF) model.
The Omeka S platform of Crossing Fonds supports the creation of case study modules that permit further connections between collections through item-level, item-set (collections of digital objects), and module access (affordances that support interaction). Items can also be connected across case studies. The designers established a set of roles that emerged through co-design workshops and persona user journeys to support a variety of users and user groups. These draw from and are limited by role capabilities of the Omeka S software. https://omeka.org/s/docs/user-manual/sites/site_users/
Ploessl, as Global Administrator, oversaw installation and site administration and acted as Site Administrator. She was joined by several other managers who could approve content and grant user permissions. Editors/Creators are content experts able to edit the site and add or verify content. These were researchers, archivists, and participating artists. A site-specific Guest category could browse items, curate their own personal collection of items, and explore and compare item sets made by other users.

Digital humanities research brings critical data studies
In What does a Critical Data Studies look like and why do we care? () Craig Dalton and Jim Thatcher initiated a still relevant analysis of the sources of data, the methods of their collection, and application.
into play with digital archival research ; ; ; ; .
Citations include authors who propose critical engagement with data (need to know how produced, by whom, for which purposes, and access) and archival remediation through collections management, description and metadata changes or additions.
Enhanced metadata description tools support understanding and reinterpretation of records and their provenance. The Omeka S design included Crossing Fonds-customized resource templates, vocabularies, and ontologies that allow users to navigate to the item (object) within Crossing Fonds and to the originating digital archive. The moderated Commenting feature (renamed to Interpretive Analysis) assigns message boards to individual item pages, allowing guests to add context via comments, with administrators able to retain or remove comments before publication. The Contributions feature supports guest users in proposing metadata suggestions which can be included or deleted by administrators and adopted by contributing archives.
The Add Item feature allows guests to submit a new item using an online form that accompanies an item; they are then required to provide and authenticate rights and permissions. Participating archives may choose to acquire the item. The Collecting feature allows guests to make their own selection of available items which can be made public and added to item sets by administrators. Researchers tested these four features in participatory design workshops that provided access to Case Study 1 to a diverse community and at a Crossing Fonds symposium and received new items from participants collections, tags, and suggestions for new data on personal lives. Participants created new item sets that combine Case Study 1 items with items in Case Study 3 (Black Cultural History in the Lower Mainland. The prototype required administrative permissions to use these features and even in a final version suggested changes to metadata that would need approval by the originating archive. In future designs, interpretive analysis would require moderation and factchecking. The current interface clearly separates commentary from metadata.

A module or item set can act as an exhibition space where smaller related item sets can be shown relationally and where Editors/Creators can invite other users to interact and comment. All categories of users can tag items with descriptive terms to support navigation by others to the items and visualization. Simple visualization can occur for example by exploring connections between items and their provenance through timelines of events and related diverse documents (newspaper clippings, minutes, testimonies). and emphasize the value of visualizing archival data to relate items and all manner of metadata associated with the item, enhance cross-referencing, and lessen cognitive load in support of analysis. Editors/Creators can develop navigable, customized Excel databases that connect items and act as filters and can be made accessible to other users. For this reason, Crossing Fonds Case Study 1 offers interactive navigation tools, a Thematic Research Guide, and an Oral History Research document that support deep dives into relationships between items and item sets from five archives, digital genealogical datasets, and newspaper collections — hence crossing fonds. Crossing Fonds offers the possibilities of associative digital memory as proposes, which is unique and distinct from physical engagement with single or even multiple objects.

div.head: Phase One – WLHP and Feminist Archival Activism
div.p: Critique, activism, and restructuring of archives bears a strong lineage in feminist historiography. The critical assessment of archives began well before the twenty-first century and formed a baseline for the Women’s Labour History Project’s engagement with collecting institutions through the 1970s to the 1990s. Absences in official archives coupled with biases inherent in their mandates, content, finding aids, and metadata descriptions led to the eventual creation of the Sara Diamond fonds as a supplemental resource, which includes the Women’s Labour History Project archives.

Feminist and feminist labour historians of the 1970s and early 1980s reflected on what was collected and excluded, including the structure of ontologies, which indicate hierarchies of description. Sheila Rowbotham contributed a cogent critique of biases and exclusions in archives. In Hidden from History: 300 Years of Women's Oppression and the Fight Against It (1973), Rowbotham argues that institutional archives working within the traditional archival framework and the resulting historical narratives have systematically excluded women’s life experience, especially those of working-class women, by focusing on public and political spheres dominated by men. She proposes that these exclusions are born of material inequities reflecting patriarchal and class-based structures that shape what is considered historically significant. Rowbotham emphasized that women's lives are underrepresented in official records and institutional archives because they are centered around domestic labour and caregiving, with resistance often expressed outside formal organizations. These concerns about exclusion find reflection decades later in the thinking of Michele Caswell in her treatise The Archive is not an Archive (2016) and in the feminist taxonomies of .

Alice Kessler-Harris, a leading twentieth-century feminist labour historian, was equally influential with the insistent 1981 monograph Women Have Always Worked: A Historical Overview. Kessler-Harris not only recovered the voices of working women but also challenged the structures and assumptions of archival and historical practice, recognizing that institutional archives excluded records representing the experiences of working, immigrant, and racialized women , . Kessler-Harris argued (; ) to broaden the types of archival sources that historians used, including oral histories, union newsletters, personal correspondence, fiction and autobiographies, and government policy documents. , , and all argue that historians must look beyond institutional archives to uncover women's histories, using sources such as personal letters, oral histories, pamphlets, and grassroot publications, which are conventionally ranked as less authoritative. in her study of records held in lesbian counter-archives, not in institutional or personal archives, documents a dilemma for women’s histories. She invokes the intensive (largely volunteer) labour required to preserve and ethically represent such records and how transmediation raises serious issues around confidentiality and women’s safety.

Reflecting the turn to positionality in social sciences and humanities — where researchers locate and disclose their social status and identities — these historians of different generations propose that there is no objective position for the researcher undertaking archival explorations . Their experience and memory will mediate responses to documents and objects. These views influence the ways that the WLHP produced revisionist histories that reconsidered both the history of women and labour and the ways their lives were represented in the records of their time.
While feminist historiography held an important influence on the research of the Women’s Labour History Project, so did British Columbian explorations of Indigenous labour as well as Canadian and regional labour history. Notable is Rolf Knight’s Indians at Work: An Informal History of Native Labour in British Columbia 1858-1930, an extensively researched analysis of the critical role of Indigenous labour in the creation of the capitalist economy of British Columbia, as well as the interventions by government and industry to decrease the power and effect of Indigenous labour. The attention to Indigenous labour is reflected across the WLHP collection and projects, and in priorities of Crossing Fonds.
These methodologies are reflected in the structure of Crossing Fonds, which enables community users to comment on metadata and items and to curate their own interpretive item sets.

WLHP strategies relied on oral histories, and then video histories a decade later, to address the lack of women’s underrepresentation in archives and library collections. Rowbotham and Kessler-Harris underscored the imperative of women’s oral histories, at best in concert with other records, but at times as the only source of history, to provide testimony, lived experience, life, and life cycle reflections.
Democratic oral history practices emerged in the UK, and Paul Thompson’s book The Voice of the Past (1978) argued that oral histories could include working class, women’s and other excluded voices.
retheorize oral histories as a negotiation between the interviewer and the subject and as an exchange of power. Attention to questions and care for the subject were critical to the practice; in contemporary terms, this is an ethics of care . Diamond and the WLHP collected life histories from the women they interviewed, with a focus on understanding what motivated women’s activism and their context, as much as the methods of organization .

figure.head: A screen capture of a media item and descriptive metadata. The WLHP interviewed Jean Sheils in the mid-1980s. Metadata refers to themes in the video and provides some biographical data. The remediation of the video excerpt from an interview clip to its recontextualization within Crossing Fonds illustrates remediation.

div.p: Early on in its work, the WLHP created and published the annotated Women’s Labour History in British Columbia: A Bibliography, 1930-1948 (1980) and an Aural (oral) history guide, Chambermaids and Whistle Punks: An Aural History of Women in B.C. Labour, 1930-55 (1982). The bibliography includes a wide range of sources, from fonds within institutional archives and libraries to feminist alternative publications, archives held by trade unions, press, journal, conference articles, book chapters, and books. These early guides are updated and provided for Crossing Fonds Case Study 1. Further, in a strategy reiterated in Case Study 1, the WLHP refused to create a hierarchy of records by recognizing oral histories, labour press, and employer archives as each playing a role within a network of positioned resources. Union records are rich sources to catalogue women’s presence, issues, and debates, but very rarely created from the perspective of women workers or organizers.

figure.head: A scan of the cover of the Women’s Labour History in British Columbia: A Bibliography, 1930-48.
A scan of pages 66 and 67 of the Bibliography illustrating its contents.

div.p: Caswell and Cifor’s (2019) theorization of ethics of care serves as both motivation and methodology for engagement with marginalized communities in the construction and interpretation of archives. What further differentiated the Women’s Labour History Project in Phase One was positioning it not only as an academic or artistic project but equally its role in creating versions of histories that could be used by community activists. The WLHP was committed to creating counter narratives. and its tactics included interpretive practices such as experimental documentaries, fictionalizations, television broadcasts, photographic exhibitions, publications, and curriculum. The WLHP’s work required forensic quests for archival footage and photographic images from the historical eras that it represented, literally dumpster diving to retrieve footage that media organizations were discarding.

The WLHP was able to build a new visual and oral archive of women’s labour by reassembling and remediating records from these archives. The WLHP then wrote original scripts inspired by historical research and sources, such as advertising and documentary scripts, and montaged photographic images and footage. proposes that these practices constitute archiveology — the reuse, recycling, appropriation, and borrowing of archival sounds and images by filmmakers provide ways to imagine the past and the future. The archive moves from a site of preservation to one of critical investigation. The WLHP’s artistic methods provided complex rereading of oral history transcripts and biographies, as , linking reinterpreted stories to historical events and shared culture. The WLHP shared its creations, exhibitions, and public readings from oral histories through union education and outreach.
WLHP researchers scoured archives for photographs, magazine illustrations, audio records, and moving images. Canada’s Library and Archives Canada film collection, National Film Board, Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (where we were literally dumpster diving when alerted to tapes from the 1940s and 1950s being thrown out), Royal BC Museum and Archives, Vancouver City Archives, BC Federation of Labour, International Woodworkers of America, and regional and personal archives provided sources that included early photographs and film footage shot by nurses, travelers, hobbyists, industry representatives, government, labour and labour activists to media institutions. These were transferred to video and then digital formats.
Samples of these works are included in the Case Study 1 item sets.

figure.head: A glossy poster advertising the WLHP’s Keeping the Home Fires Burning video series. A black and white photo dominates the poster. A black and white video still of a young woman playing a 1940s worker collaged over an archival photo of a protest. Descriptive text frames the photo on two sides.

div.p: Three feminist digital archive projects are rooted in the need to surface absent activist histories and offer complementary transmediation approaches to the WLHP’s efforts. Fuerza Feminista, Chicana por mi Raza, and the Domestic Workers Timeline embody cultures of care, respectful data collection and organization, and effective site navigation strategies. All projects have links to relevant organizations, as did the WLHP in its ties to feminist unionism, and more recently Crossing Fonds and the CDMLA in their collaboration with the BC Labour Heritage Centre.

Sylvia Fernández and Cynthia Bejarano began Fuerza Feminista: Intimate Recovery of Memory Archive (FFIRMA) in 2019. FFIRMA provides documentation of thirty years of gender-based violence in the Mexican state of Chihuahua, bordering Texas and New Mexico, and resistance to it by local communities. Fernández and Cynthia Bejarano develop tools and methodologies for feminist data and digital humanities scholars, activist-scholars, and others to utilize when documenting and analyzing crimes against humanity . As was true of the WLHP in its original phase, their research challenges “intersectional data violence” to address data inaccuracies and absences which appear in official records, combining personal records with public accounts to identify and defend victims of femicide.
Fernández and Bejarano argue that to confront IDV, it is important to collect data and metadata that center intimate archives with care and responsibility and to also create archives in a slow manner through a long-term commitment and with an ethics of mutuality . This ethical process of data gathering, intimate archiving, fits the WLHP longitudinal history, including their return to interview subjects over several decades (1970s through the 1990s) in the comfort of their homes, sharing recordings with participants, care taken in the disclosure of personal information, and Crossing Fonds' efforts at redescription of inaccurate metadata.

María Eugenia Cotera and Linda Garcia Merchant’s Chicana por mi Raza project documents the labor, activism, and social justice work of Chicana women during the Chicano rights movement, through personal and collective archives, creating a community-based feminist archive. It was created in collaboration with The Institute for Computing in Humanities Arts and Sciences at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. The archive includes over 80 oral histories and thousands of personal documents. Like Diamond’s stated positionality within the WLHP as a labour organizer, and her efforts to situate women unionists within a broader male-dominated labour movement, Cotera and Garcia Merchant’s initiative is motivated by their personal histories of activism and familial relationship to the Chicano rights movement. They frame this work as centering collaboration, reciprocity, relatedness, and a shared obligation to the past, present, and future, which creates space to write with the past rather than about it . Archival interface design is comprised of subsites that delve deeply into incidents and movements. This strategy echoes the CDMLA’s effective narrative sub-curation of collections, such as the Women & West Coast Labour, in which subsites serve as both organizational tools and gateways. It relies on navigable digital tools and includes timelines and story map visualizations of Chicana activism (women engaged with the Chicano movement). Like the WLHP’s narrative video works, the resulting recovered historias [stories] act as transmediations of archival artifacts and oral histories so that we can reconstruct rich retellings of important actions and moments in Chicana activist history that have been otherwise omitted from the record . A goal of this work is to achieve a better understanding of the present and look forward to embracing a relation of knowledge production in which the present and the past are in active dialogue .

Smith College’s Guglielmo and Joffroy (, ) developed The Domestic Workers Timeline with the National Domestic Workers Alliance. It presents a timeline visualization to navigate the complex history of domestic service and resistance from pre-Conquest times to the present, with a first version completed in 2018 and an updated version in 2021 (https://dwherstories.com/). They note, This timeline documents the history of domestic work and organizing in the United States. It demonstrates how control over domestic workers has been key to the rise and consolidation of oppressive systems. It also captures how domestic workers personally and collectively experienced exploitation and oppression (. Rather than an archive, it draws from secondary sources listed in its bibliography, which are summarized with text and audio clips that are linked to the timeline. A film version of these histories was added in 2021. Given the close relationship of domestic labour to restaurant and hotel labour, this resource further situates the archival materials and histories presented in Crossing Fonds and discussed in this article. The fine-tuned timeline navigation strategy provides a model for future development of the Crossing Fonds OMEKA S site.

Case Study 1 offered several opportunites: return to source archival documents from the early work of the WLHP; transmediate these into digital forms; include early analytic texts by Diamond, other team members, and historians from the period; search for new relationships and interpretations or reinforcements of previous analysis; and create new tools.
For example, You Can't Scare Me. I'm Stickin' to the Union: Women in British Columbia During the Great Depression was written by Diamond for Kenesis a feminist magazine and published in 1979 (https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/1282) and the original oral history collection guide is included (https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/374). It can be situated as a contribution to contemporary feminist archival practices.

div.head: Phase Two – Bringing the WLHP/Diamond fonds to VIVO Media Arts
div.p: Diamond donated her fonds to the CDMLA in 2018, situating the materials that were created while Diamond lived in Vancouver within the context of, and in dialogue with, mixed media collections of other Vancouver feminist artists, collectives, and movements, many of which had collegial and overlapping histories. For VIVO, the acquisition was significant for its recognition of Diamond as an innovator and influencer in Vancouver’s cultural and academic communities, and as an educator and curator at Video Inn (now VIVO) in the 1980s. As importantly, Diamond is a critical figure in the history of feminist early adopters of portable audio and video recording technologies that would become ubiquitous tools for the documentation and reframing of experience and ideas through a feminist lens. Recordings were shared through women’s groups, community centres, artist-run centres, LGBTQ organizations, alternative media distributors, community television and radio, media festivals venues that in the 1970s through the 1990s were building rich, counter-archives for the feminist and marginalized voices that Caswell, Kessler-Harris, and others, found absent from institutional archives.

Since the early 1970s, Canadian media-focused artist-run centres (ARCs), like VIVO, took the initiative to collect analog and, later, born-digital media representing the cultural and political activities of marginalized communities. From the 1980s, in a collective act of transmediation, ARCs developed sophisticated and “good-enough” media migration and preservation protocols for video. These digital collections fill a vital gap in the historical record left by institutional archives that were late to collecting the histories of and by marginalized communities, especially those who were working in analog video.

div.head: Creating rich (generous) interfaces: philosophy and examples
div.p: The CDMLA began experimenting with putting their archival videos online in 2015. In 2018, as part of the CDMLA’s push to make the Sara Diamond fonds publicly accessible, Knights initiated a project using digital access, navigation, and generous interfaces , . Mitchell Whitelaw (, ) called for generous archives, a radical resetting of archival finding aides and interfaces that breaks with the reading room metaphor of collections hidden behind a search box and that instead encourages liberal sharing of archival holdings (), including cultural collections () that display rich visual content with deep browsable views while providing contextual awareness and relationships.

The curated online exhibition Women & West Coast Labour: Eighty years of action for equity in domestic and workplace labour by Women in British Columbia launched on the VIVO archive site in 2019. Accessible at: https://archive.vivomediaarts.com/women-and-west-coast-labour/
Digitization of Diamond’s fonds contributed: video and audio oral histories; production photographs and photographs donated from interviewees’ personal collections; educational resources developed through Diamond’s research; and relevant interviews with Diamond. The fonds also contributed work by Amelia Productions, a feminist documentary video and fiction film collective, and interviews with labour activists by Jean Sheils, a long-term political activist. These were linked through a visually rich generous interface. This is equally a form of transmediation, in which modes of perception are reconfigured, rather than preserved .

The WLHP collection is complimented in the online exhibition by the collection of Vancouver’s first feminist media centre, Women in Focus (WIF). The WIF fonds contributed episodes of their community cable television show, film and video documentaries and narrative works (1974-1980), media catalogues, political leaflets on workplace harassment, and photographs documenting the labour of the WIF collective. In their examination of women’s working lives in the 1970s, the WIF materials reiterated the historical conditions and struggles of women workers that can be traced back through Diamond’s interviews.

Audiences browsing the online exhibition could imagine the relationships between the two collections and their objects. However, unlike Crossing Fonds, participants could not move or regroup objects across these distinct but thematically related fonds. The online exhibition benefitted from a significant digital file exchange between Simon Fraser University Archives and the CDMLA and the enriched metadata that were connected through one site; this exchange hinted at the archival aggregation strategy and generous interface design that would be represented fully in the Crossing Fonds platform. Through the course of the project, online access to the Sara Diamond fonds inspired new partnerships, including several substantive and ongoing digital exhibition collaborations with The British Columbia Labour Heritage Centre (BCLHC), a community based historical society and partner on the Crossing Fonds project.

div.head: Phase Three – Crossing Fonds Case Study 1
div.p:
Knights and Diamond worked on Case Study 1 as Editors/Creator of the emerging platform, the former as a community archivist and the other as an historian, as well as a donor of one of the source fonds and Principal Investigator of Crossing Fonds. Building on the previous phases of the WLHP, their overall goal was to create a collaborative workspace for researchers, artists, and non-academic community members. Salmose & Elleström propose that transmediation is about ‘picking out’ elements from a medium and using them in a new way in another medium . The platform itself was a transmediation of previous ways of presenting these archives, preserving original content while transferring medium, shifting semiotics, and engaging with raw and mediated data in a respectful feminist context.
Peña and Kedrick helpfully describe the fungibility of the concept of transmediation, and its ability to include sensory, semiotic, signal, raw data and medium transformation.
Diamond and Knights hoped 1) to experiment with the Omeka S interface and its modules, craft the process of collecting archival items into a unified digital space, find ways to interact with materials from multiple sources and of multiple media types, and create new relationships; 2) to cultivate new interpretations of the histories represented through the records uploaded and organized on the platform; 3) to build a set of interactive tools that both supported the research and that other users of the collaborative space would find of value; 4) to create coherence within the case study item sets to provide a meaningful, if not fully interactive experience, for public users, including public presentations; and 5) to provide opportunities for other users to comment on, enhance, and correct the records in the fonds as a further step of transmediation.

div.head: Building Case Study 1
div.p: Case Study 1 considered the broader context of work, society, and labour organization in the 1930s, 1940s, and 1970s. These decades were chosen by the researchers because of their significant differences in service sector demographics, working conditions, political formations, and forms of labour organization, such as craft, industrial, and independent feminist and Indigenous unionism. These periods were also chosen in part because of the range of relevant archived diverse media in collections and that the WLHP fonds and the HREU fonds were distributed across multiple archives.

The above considerations informed the Creator/Editor research team Diamond and Knights’ decisions around structuring the research for Crossing fonds. Case Study 1 is divided into four primary item sets, one with four sub-sets within it.

div.head: Case Study 1 primary item sets
div.p:
SORWUC 1970s-1980s: An item set regarding the Service Office and Retail Workers Union of Canada, a feminist union representing service and finance sector workers, and Indigenous workers.
Collections reside in UBC Special Collections and in the Diamond fonds which includes pamphlets, support from the companion union Association of University and College Employees and women’s movement materials (https://archive.vivomediaarts.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/Sara-Diamond-fonds_Finding-Aid.pdf), (https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/page/sorwuc-1970s-1980s). Records originate from Diamond’s fonds at the CDMLA, SFU Archives, and UBC Special Collections.
Details of the UBC collection are available here: https://guides.library.ubc.ca/labourhistoryarchives/sorwuc.
SORWUC led a significant and highly publicized strike at the Muckamuck, a restaurant featuring Indigenous food and an all-Indigenous staff but owned by wealthy international art dealers Jane Erikson and Doug Christmas.
See: https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/1081. The Province details the party (October 11, 1978, p. 44).

HREU 1930s-1940s: Includes items from the HREU Local 28 fonds from multiple archives (City of Vancouver Archives, UBC Special Collections, the CDMLA); researchers notes from the HREU minutes; Vancouver District Trade and Labour Council (VDTLC) minutes which contextualize the larger labour movement; HREU International minutes items regarding British Columbia and international locals.
https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/page/hreu-1930s-1940s is the overview of both item sets.
There are personal testimonies (oral and video recordings), press clippings of strikes and political conflicts, and documentation of the role of the HREU in labour policy.
Overall navigation is enabled from this page: https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/page/hreu-1930s-1940s. A strength of OMEKA S is the ability to effectively divide item sets into meaningful groupings.
There are digitized ephemera such as union cards and buttons.
Background Documents: This item set constitutes a selection of information on the case study topic, including archival materials and academic historical publications.

Researchers Guides and Notes: This item set includes the Thematic Guide for Case Study 1 records core data on the research resources and as a guide for other researchers
The Thematic Guide can be used to navigate the site or downloaded (https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/438) and the extensive Oral History Research documents.

HREU 1930s-1940s were organized further with subsets:Restaurant Organizing: Items pertaining to restaurant organizing from the 1930s to the 1940s.Hotel Organizing: Items pertaining to hotel organizing from the 1930s to the 1940s.Communism and Unions: Items pertaining to HREU Local 28’s rocky affiliation with the Vancouver Trades and Labour Council and its international union, and the intense internecine struggle between political factions. Anti-Asian Racism: Items pertaining to campaigns against white women working in “Chinatown cafes,” resistance by waitresses, the history of anti-Asian legislation and campaigns, including within the labour movement.

Rather than create a unified item set of all hotel and restaurant organizing, SORWUC and HREU records were separated to invite comparison between organizing in the 1970s and the 1930s-1940s. SORWUC’s history is also distinct because of its focus on feminist unionism as detailed by Smith (2015) and its engagement with Indigenous workers and communities and their rights not only as workers but as Indigenous culture bearers (Nicol, 1997).

The Site Administrator Ploessl provided the Case Study 1 team with access to the back end of the Omeka S platform to add and manage items. Omeka S provides Creator/Editors with the choice to bulk upload (via CSV) or to create stand-alone items. Manual item addition is often employed if the collection is small, or, in the case of the Sara Diamond fonds, does not have existing item-level descriptions. The manual feature also allowed the Creator/Editors to add items on an ad hoc basis. All items were included in the Case Study 1 Parent Set (a container for all items uploaded for that case study).

Resource Templates (preset combinations of metadata fields) determine the basic structure of the item record. A Creator/Editor can choose a preset best suited to their collection or object. The Case Study 1 researchers chose media-specific resource templates (i.e. Moving Image, Document, Sound). AV records (video and audio files), while unique resource templates, integrate into an item set. Ease of uploading and integrating media was a critical requirement in the design of the platform. The Creator/Editor can also add specialized vocabularies, ontologies, and more, hence a relevant feature for Case Study 1, was that descriptive metadata can easily be revised by the team, which became a critical feature for the reinterpretation, correction, or enhancement of metadata for any item. The WLHP was attentive to issues of racism and Indigenous representation in their work decades earlier, and documents considering racism and Indigenous contributions to labour are included in the item sets. The platform offered the opportunity to reframe Diamond and her WLHP colleagues’ decades-old description of Indigenous and other materials in revised metadata notes. The Crossing Fonds project included Indigenous and racialized community membership within the research and archival staff teams, and description was shared widely. For example, Diamond clarified that she collected Indigenous oral histories and documents in the 1970s as a labour activist, in collaboration with Indigenous family members. Oral histories were again returned to the families.

An integrated media importer allows multiple discrete media items (across types) to be linked to each item. These items can be components of a larger item, for instance, the aggregation of twenty discrete spreadsheets that make up the Oral History Research document or a variety of media related to the core item. Each item is associated with an Item Set(s) ( a collection of items "Item sets" as a term comes much earlier in this article. Would you want to move the definition to an earlier instance?
Yes, great idea. It is a fundamental structuring method for Omeka) for organizational or display purposes. The researchers defined item sets by subject, theme, date, or creator.

The team created primary item records (detailed later in this essay) which included rich metadata descriptions as well as discussions of relationships with other items and their context. While item records are common in digital archives, Crossing Fonds supported a generous archives strategy where notes were displayed alongside item and item sets. These formed the basis for Comments and Contributions for metadata corrections and enhancements.

div.head: Metadata Description and Explanatory Notes
div.p: OMEKA S provides a beneficial range of metadata values, including text entries and bi-directional links, provenance, media description, customized tags, and categories. Waugh (2020) emphasizes the opportunity that digital archives offer for rich metadata description for discoverability and context provision. The research team provided enhanced or corrected (Frederick, S. 2019) metadata description on an item-by-item basis.

The researchers also utilized the facility to create custom Research Collection sub-sets to represent a theme, for example, an individual or trade union action. An overarching Research Collection record is created under which sub-set the unique items are organized. Like all items and item sets, it allows custom descriptive metadata. The flexibility of the descriptive fields encourages researchers to use them for whatever purpose they feel serves the set. In addition to descriptive metadata, a Creator/Editor can add notes about the metadata, contextual information, or, in the case of guides, instructions on how to use and navigate them. Research Collections can be used to organize records (i.e., a chronological mapping of correspondence)
The “HREU Local 28 1947 Executive Expulsion: November 6,8,9 1947” item set is derived from the collection of Local 28 Secretary Business Agent, May (Leniczek) Martin which was donated to Sara Diamond. This collection that documents the communist purge undertaken by the International fills the gap in the Local 28 records available at the City of Vancouver and UBC Archives. It illustrates the value of the Crossing Fonds platform that brings together institutional, community, and personal archives. See https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/1345
or to recontextualize disparate items. The latter can illuminate how the actions of government, unions, employers impact women’s personal and professional lives; or surface new information about union organizing.
https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/1265 details the strike at the Crescent restaurant. Women won better wages. This may also have been the first Chinese owned restaurant that the HREU organized. Coverage by The Lumber Worker provides the tactics of the striking waitresses and how the HREU negotiated with a reluctant employer and can be contrasted with the Province coverage. Item description provides details on the history and comparative documentation
One example is the “HREU Local 28 1947 Executive Expulsion: November 6, 8, 9 1947” item set that assembles union correspondence, meeting minutes, and legal documents related to a critical confrontation between HREU International and Officers of Local 28. It includes handwritten minutes of a “Citizen’s Meeting” following the cancellation of a Local 28 meeting that same day by the HREU International. The minutes document a motion carried by the attendees to resign from Local 28 and form an independent union.

Researchers created an Oral Histories Research document. The multi-sheet XLS workbook consists of three types of data sheets. These are Object (listing each archival item related to the biographical subject), Subject (the interviewee’s biographical data including birthdates, immigration status, gender expectations, etc.), and Research Notes (one sheet per interviewee with select excerpts from the interview(s) that record “relevant occurrences” which are core observations or experiences of the interviewee directly related to research questions such as: strategies for organizing women workers in British Columbia, domestic life, supportive and related social and political movements. The metadata describes the guide and how to use it. Additional notes deploy genealogical research to inform the biographies.

div.head: Supporting Commentary and Metadata Revision
div.p: Critical archival practices include reinterpreting content through the correction and annotation of original metadata and descriptions of archival holdings to better represent equity-seeking groups whose records exist in archives. This practice is at times described as decolonizing description and attribution and can accompany the return of archives to originating communities (Allison-Cassin, 2020; Anderson & Christen, 2019; Luker, 2017; Doyle et al., 2015; Farnel et al., 2015). Crossing Fonds held a series of description workshops led by Dr. Andrea Fatona (OCAD U) and participatory design workshops led by Dr. Sheelagh Carpendale (SFU), Melanie Hardbattle (SFU Archives) and Andrea Tarnawsky (SFU Library) which supported participants — historians, archivists, librarians, artists, members of the Indigenous community — in using the Comments (retitled to “Interpretive Analysis”) and Contribution features to describe and rewrite metadata descriptions, comment on items within an item set, and upload relevant items to item sets. We plan to expand opportunities to share these histories and gather commentary and metadata interpretation suggestions with contemporary organized hotel and restaurant workers in collaboration with BCLHC.

div.head: Thematic Guide
div.p:
The Thematic Guide for Case Study 1 was inspired by the Women’s Labour History in British Columbia: A Bibliography, 1930-1948 (1980). It records core data on the research resources for analysis and serves as a guide for other researchers.
The Thematic Guide can be used to navigate the site or downloaded: https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/438
It is currently in prototype form. Archival arrangement has traditionally been organized by provenance (the creator of the fonds, usually an individual, organization, company, or family). Fonds may comprise materials on one subject or many. In the post-digital era, some archives have supplemented traditional finding aids (often a hierarchical inventory of the collection with series descriptions and file lists) with curated finding aids or research guides that provide a scan of materials across fonds on a particular subject or theme. These are increasingly web-based and searchable and link to items at online digital repositories. They are tailored to research trends and public interests and are editable.

VIVO’s archivists developed two curated, searchable, online thematic guides for CDMLA prior to Crossing Fonds: “Every Queer Thing: A Subject Guide to Archival Materials on Queer Identity and Experience” (2020)
https://archive.vivomediaarts.com/every-queer-thing “Every Queer Thing: A Subject Guide to Archival Materials on Queer Identity and Experience” Sophie Roberge (MAS/MLIS), CDMLA Archivist in Residence, 2019.
and “Presence – A Research Guide to Indigenous Materials at the CDMLA” (2021).
https://archive.vivomediaarts.com/presence “Presence – A Research Guide to Indigenous Materials at the CDMLA” Syr Reifsteck (MAS/MLIS), 2021.
The first guide expanded production metadata to acknowledge worker and community contributions. The second expanded fields to surface Indigenous content, language, place, and creators not included in the original descriptive metadata. Users were able to select their fields of interest, search for keywords, and download the data in multiple formats.

Weideman (2019) argues that Thematic Guides can be counterproductive, directive, and at times substituted for rigorous cataloguing, which inhibits standardization and rich metadata. Addressing these concerns, Case Study 1’s Thematic Guide facilitates individual and collaborative study through a centralized, sharable interface. It comprises metadata (original and/or generated by the research team) and enhanced context for digital objects sourced from academic, governmental, and community archives. It provides fields intended to surface new contexts that are relevant to transmediation, for example, how technologies may inform a reading of the object. The categories listed below manage source and location data for the object and provide linked access to institutions, collections, creator, and the digital object. Additional fields describe the object’s unique traits and context relevant to the theme. In total, the guide allows for comparative analysis across multiple sources and illustrates pathways to further analysis.

div.head: Guided by the Guides: Learnings Enabled by Crossing Fonds
div.p:
Crossing Fonds allowed Diamond and Knights to gain a deeper understanding of the extreme working conditions of restaurant workers. By seeking entries in the Thematic Guide and Oral History Research document, searching and comparing records from the HREU and the Vancouver and District Labour Trades and Council (VDTLC), reviewing digitized artifacts, including oral and video histories and press coverage, Diamond and Knights learned of workers’ tactics towards establishing and sustaining a union house (restaurant) in the face of harassment and low pay, sometimes seven days a week for as long as ten hours per day and split shifts. Union cards and labels designated union houses. Workers were expected to carry union cards to prove they were paying dues and were checked and fined if they did not comply; in turn, the local placed women into restaurants, giving members priority. HREU consistently appealed to the VDTLC for unionists to frequent unionized restaurants and boycott anti-union employers. Minutes record arguments over non-compliance. Union activity was characterized by spontaneous strikes and work-to-rule actions because of the use of non-union labour and poor conditions.
Vancouver District Trades and Labour Council Minutes, 1938
Yet the efforts of HREU organizers and activists, connected through these records, saw the local grow from thirty-five card-carrying members in 1935 to the third largest member of the VDTLC by 1938, made up of eighty percent women.
See extensive researchers’ notes from HREU minutes: https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/1295
Women increasingly took up the torch as organizers for HREU with campaigns and strikes throughout the decade of the 1940s as women returned to service jobs after the war.

Hotel organizing campaigns were orchestrated and achieved by Emily Nutall and May Martin (Leniczek; Ansell) (Back row L-R) Margaret Shelton, Chairman [sic] of Education and Publicity and Gertrude Philip, Chairman of the Social Committee. (Front row L-R) Arabella Beck, Recording Secretary; Emily Watts, President; May Ansell, Secretary Treasurer and Business Agent. and escalated in the immediate post-war period resulting in a national agreement.
See May Martin, Barbara Stewart, Emily Nutall, Susie Fawcett, and Daisy Brown interviews. These also show some of the political divides in the local: https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/502; https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/1188; https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/857; https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/366 ; https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/508 and the Oral Histories Research document https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/963.
The Hotel Organizing sub-item set allows researchers to examine the list of organized hotels and the full agreement, read engaging and passionate testimonies from organizers and press coverage, and find evidence of the contradictory ways that these successes were reported and received by the labour movement.
See the list of unionized hotels by 1947: https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/876
Analysis across these documents allows a timeline to emerge, pinpointing individual organizers, key actions, and shifting attitudes. On the one hand, women faced paternalism, expressed in minutes of the VDTLC; on the other, they built a powerful union, under almost impossible conditions, all of which are expressed in minutes of the HREU.

Violence against women was an issue for women working in the restaurant sector and foregrounded by the HREU in the 1930s and 1940s. Case Study 1 linked government policy documents, union minutes, testimonials, and press clippings to show the arc of proposed remedies. Reformers, including women’s rights advocates, debated whether to restrict women to day work to protect them against violence when leaving late shifts, while union women fought for better transportation and late-night policing as they had no choice but to work and to walk home. After the murder of waitress Olga Hawryluk on May 2, 1945, the labour movement supported legislation to require employers to provide safe transport for night shift workers. These views contradicted earlier labour movement policies to restrict shift work for women.
https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/730: A newspaper article documenting the HREU (AFL)'s call for changes to shift work in cafes and restaurants, following Hawryluk’s murder by a customer following a night shift. This article is notable for impassioned statements from Emily Watts (HREU organizer), and May Ansell (HREU Business Agent) despite Hawryluk not being a union member. https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/1253: “VDTLC Minutes - Research selection 1944–1946” include discussions on night shift hour changes.
The linked documents connected minutes of the HREU, press clippings and WLHP oral histories. These starkly illuminated the direct connections between media representation of the tragedies, the resulting public outcry, and the union’s ability to leverage these concerns to force employers’ action to improve women’s safety.

Researchers used both guides and a wide array of items to grasp the profound internecine warfare between HREU Local 28’s Communist and progressive Vancouver leadership and the conservative American HREU international and its representatives in the Vancouver and District Labour Council. Crossing Fonds for the first time brings together competing sets of HREU records. This previously untold story is richly illuminated by a trove of digitized original documents given to Diamond by Martin
Diamond had ensured redundancy of the oral histories through deposits at the BC Archive, Simon Fraser Archives, and VIVO Media Arts Centre. The original documents reside at VIVO’s archive. In “Exclusion or Solidarity: Vancouver Workers Confront the Oriental Problem” Gillean Creese writes about these contradictory approaches: https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/934
from her personal archives.
Minutes and notes from minutes provide an overview of the tensions, expulsions and returns of Communist leaders (https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/896 and https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/1371) as do selected minutes (https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/1260). Researcher notes show the gaps from periods where there were changes in leadership and the business of the local was suspended (https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/1295). Notes from labour history sources provide a larger British Columbia and Canadian context (https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/924).
Records relate to the Vancouver HREU business office takeover by leaders Emily Nuttall and May Martin in 1947 after they were removed from union leadership. Examples include a variety of escalating letters between the HREU 28 leaders and the HREU International (who described the women as insurrectionists), annotated minutes from competing union sources, court documents, financial records and convention documents (expulsion was in part predicated by the Canadian caucus’s support of an alternative leader for the International at the Milwaukee Convention).
https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/1345 provides letters between the two factions. These records are notably from May Martin records that she donated to Diamond and reside in her fonds at CDLMA. https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/1391 provides Canadian caucus minutes and are also from the Martin items. https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/1374 includes newspaper coverage of the convention.
These items allow researchers to decipher the history of the union local within the larger contemporaneous labour context. These item sets enable a day-by-day account of the crisis. The evidence was so compelling that it inspired a physical exhibition of digital and scanned artifacts as part of the Crossing Fonds Symposium exhibitions at VIVO.

Racism was a virulent force in British Columbia and in Greater Vancouver during the decades of this case study, fueled by fears of competition for jobs, jealousy regarding economic gains by Chinese and Japanese communities, and xenophobic beliefs in white supremacy. Case Study 1 follows the efforts on the part of city officials to ban white women working in Chinese owned restaurants in Vancouver’s Chinatown, ostensibly over concerns for their moral purity. Advocates for restrictions succeeded despite resistance by the waitresses who launched a public campaign and the HREU who supported the right to workDismissed Girls Parade To City Hall (Sep 25, 1937) for these non-unionized women waitresses.
https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/1496: This item represents a spokesperson for the non-unionized waitresses and includes newspaper articles, police reports, and other objects related to this dispute.
Theme sets in Case Study 1 provide a wide range of documents, including census records, government policy (such as “An Act for the Protection of Girls and Women in Certain Cases”),
https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/904: PDF of this restrictive legislation giving significant discretionary power to police to determine if a business in immoral.
café licenses, minutes, press clippings, theses, and oral histories. It included supplementary scholarship regarding Chinese women and their labour with links to oral history interviews. Canadian labour historians Star Rosenthal (1979) and Gillean Creese (1989) documented the anti-Orientalism that divided the labour movement and excluded Chinese workers who, like women, wanted to join unions but were excluded. Relevant academic analyses of women’s labour histories are provided and linked as references to original documents.
Sheila Lewenhak who wrote Women and the Trade Unions (1977) considered Britain’s definitive history of feminist labour activism, consulted archival resources while again noting absences of valuable records.
The range of documents prove that anti-Asian sentiment was a plank of organized labour throughout the 19th and early 20th centuries, although records show that by the 1930s and 1940s there were individuals and organizations in stark contrast, such as the Communist Party and Canadian Commonwealth Federation (CCF) who spoke out against racism and attempted to organize Chinese workers (Creese, 1989). Researchers built a timeline that is integrated into the sub-item set and indicates the dynamics of this campaign.
See the timeline at: https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/959
In the broader context of North American labour history, this item set echoes Rowbotham and Kessler-Harris’ documentation of labour dynamics and race in twentieth century USA.

Linked rich metadata description supports analysis of photographic collections of working women held by various archives. Over the decades (1930s–1970s) union workers began to photograph themselves in social, work, and family contexts and share these images. These photographs that were contributed to the WLHP fonds from personal archives contrast with those created by industrial and labour photographers. Metadata description notes photographic technology of these varied image sources, helping to explain this shift in authorship.
The Sara Diamond Archives includes documentation of this project: https://archive.vivomediaarts.com/the-working-image/

div.head: Crossing Fonds Case Study 1: Expanded Feminist Biographical Research
div.p: The Omeka S platform supports expanded biographical research (O’Neill et al., 2015), that is, the exploration of the history of the women who were featured in the audio and video recordings as union activists and in the larger framework of their work and social context. Feminist biography in context has been a consistent thread of all three phases of the Women’s Labour History Project. From its outset, WLHP researchers hoped to examine the ways that a critical consciousness developed in individuals and social groupings to trace the interaction of material and ideational structures which underpin personal identity and activities. This corresponds to a view of history as a dynamic process, where conflict produces constant change.

The Oral History Research document, described previously, is composed of information extracted from Case Study 1’s primary source, the WLHP’s oral histories. Biographical details and interviewee quotes were transferred to each interviewee’s data sheet and sorted chronologically under categories representing research questions. It surfaced pivotal employment and union affiliations, chronicled strategies used by employers and trade unions to control conditions within the workplace, and provided details related to research questions that were asked in the 1980s and ones relevant to feminist historiography today. lxxxi The document also surfaced data gaps, including changing domestic status and identity, long-term employment patterns, race, and lives, and, for some, details of domestic life, sexuality, and their economic and social context relative to their demographic. Recent feminist historiography of women and work emphasizes the role of women in paid and unpaid domestic labour and socialization, reinforcing earlier analyses but adding heightened awareness of intersectionality (Ferguson, 2019).

div.head: Applying Genealogical Methodology to Case Study 1
div.p: As with any qualitative source, the oral histories have nuance and context. It was important to understand actual incidents the interviews were referring to when memory was not specific or contradicted other sources. The researchers undertook extensive cross-referencing with union minutes, including placing Vancouver District Labour Council (VDLC) minutes against Hotel and Restaurant Employees Unions Local 28 (HREU) minutes and examining press and relevant fonds. The oral histories in turn enhanced the minimal information about women trade unionists found in union records and revealed key incidents unrecorded in these. The researchers' intention was to surface information that existed in tension and find new sources that further examination pointed to.

This prompted the inclusion of digital genealogical and demographic research that Knights added to the Oral History sheets and provided as separate items for individual biographies. Knights used professional genealogical methods (Smith, 2018; Shown Mills, 2018) to verify and supplement oral history demographic, employment, and biographical metadata, using publicly available online digital databases. In the past twenty years, there has been a dramatic increase in the breadth and quantity of records digitized and aimed at the amateur genealogy market. Professional genealogical research strategies and proof standards were applied to family history research. Methods used in this research derived from Professional Genealogy: Preparation, Practice & Standards (edited by Elizabeth Shown Mills, Genealogy Publishing Company. Baltimore, Maryland. 2018). These included
Ancestry.com (a subscription library of 65 billion digital records as of 2024) and the free-access, non-profit FamilySearch.org.
the largest genealogical platforms holding indexed digital records of socio-economic, migration, and demographic data across centuries. This work was attentive to concerns about the ways that genealogical narratives are constructed using assumptions about gender and gender expectations (Smith, 2018). The WLHP records and deeper research into union movements at times acted as a counter narrative to genealogical records. Obituaries and vital records (death and marriage) de-emphasized or erased women’s work and activist history and emphasized women’s ongoing role as homemakers, while oral histories and union records shone the light on a period of activism in their lives. Employing genealogical databases raises McKinney’s concerns regarding privacy and safety. Crossing Fonds is both a public-facing display platform and a private research space. Sandboxes can be used to keep sensitive research materials private.

Building a basic family tree Interviewee, parents, grandparents (and further back if necessary to establish ethnic origin), domestic partners, children (relevant years). for each interviewee provided linked access to data sets and document images, including source citations. Trees were created to surface documents that contributed to meeting genealogical proof standards. Where information was found that informed the oral histories, it was included in the Subject Guide. Secondary information like names and identifying vital statistics related to ancestors were not. This data resolved many of the gaps and inaccuracies in demographic data and enhanced context, and it matched accurate timelines to biographical recounting in the oral histories. When available, data regarding wages and other employment conditions expanded or corrected data relevant to the case study for all WLHP oral histories. Research supplemented individual women’s narrations and historical records and permitted the identification of women unionists who were not part of the original network of interviewees. Diamond and Knights applied these techniques to understand a group of twenty-four HREU members, not included in the original interviews, who had worked in advocacy or administrative roles by serving on committees, as delegates, or on the Executive during the same period as those interviewed. Only their names and periods of involvement as recorded in the HREU minutes were available. Digital genealogical tools surfaced sufficient data for 71% of this group, and demographic data was consistent with those interviewed. The Crossing Fonds item set “Researchers Guides and Notes” includes an example of a biographical chart created for one of these individuals: “HREU Women Leaders - Florence Lucy nee Allen (1898-1960).”
https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/1512: Researchers Guides and Notes: HREU Women Leaders Florence Lucy nee Allen - Biographical Data. Using city directories supplemented with scattered mentions in union records it was possible to identify her employment history between 1918 and 1960.
Allen was a waitress, HREU member (1919-1955), Local Joint Executive Board Executive, and the first Lifetime Member of the Hotel and Restaurant Employees Union Local 28. She was also on the Executive during both purges of communists from HREU Local 28. The research chart is informed by a Death Notice providing new information on her HREU career; the Omeka S platform supports the combination of these discrete items. https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/1512: This chart is uploaded to the platform and is one example of 30 charts nearing completion.

Researchers applied genealogical research that challenged the limited narrative visible in the archival record. Looking into the spare archival traces of the campaign against non-unionized white waitresses working in Chinatown, Diamond and Knights located a single document related to the waitresses’ public spokesperson, Kay Martin. The Mayor and Chief Police Commissioner were using a police report to slander Martin and other protesters. Building a full biographical profile of Martin using common genealogical datasets, the research revealed a strongly supported counternarrative exposing municipal and policing biases against the poorer and racialized population, and working women, on Vancouver’s Eastside.

In an effort to represent the experience of racialized waitresses in Vancouver of the period, researchers applied the same genealogy research techniques as they had to the core group of interviewees. Researchers found that this methodology did not yield sufficient data to contribute to findings, despite new digital tools.
https://omeka.crossingfonds.com/s/crossing-fonds/item/1426: This item includes searches of the 1931 census using new Ancestry handwriting recognition tools show anonymized results for Vancouver and New Westminster districts for women in the restaurant sector by occupation, work categories, and were identified as Black, Japanese, or Chinese under the "racial origin" category. See the attached "Bulletin No XXII, Population of Canada, 1931, By Racial Origins" for more details on how the 1931 Census represented these.
This result reflects, in part, the racist and classist structures of early 20th-century demographic procedures. Local histories, community memory, newspaper accounts, and vital records were also included in the research; however, most references to racialized women working in the restaurant industry either criminalized or degraded them. The research team included anonymized 1931 census data to the Researchers Guides and Notes item set to illustrate how Indigenous, Black, and women of colour are excluded from common research sources. To avoid reproducing racist biases, the descriptive metadata note explains the challenges with the census process of that time and the inbuilt biases. The Crossing Fonds platform supports participants from marginalized groups to upload their own data and records. Case Study 1 and Case Study 3 (Black Labour and Cultural History in the Greater Vancouver Area) addressed these gaps by collecting and adding personal family histories.

This assemblage of biographical and professional data helps stitch together a stronger and more layered understanding of the individual women. Researchers hoped to cultivate new interpretations of the histories represented through the records uploaded and organized on the platform and to build a set of interactive tools that both supported the research and that other users of the collaborative space would find of value. Humanities researchers may find value through access to genealogical and demographic data on the site.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: This essay draws on over four decades of transmediated feminist archival studies, predicated in the early work of the Women’s Labour History Project. Over the years, WLHP research has enacted “transmediation” through iterated approaches to archival items, data, and interfaces. Phase One sought to identify and describe, in part through bibliographic annotation, the presence of working women in the archival collections of its time. It supplemented official records with oral and video histories and community-created materials. It reused archival materials to produce experimental video interpretation of the past. These included experimental documentaries, fictionalizations, and exhibitions that remediated and transmediated archival content, like thematic web sites. Phase Two continued with “generous interfaces” of navigable digital documents that were created by CDMLA at VIVO to explore the WLHP within the Diamond collection and its sister collection, Women in Focus. Phase Three saw the creation of a collaborative Omeka S case study that provided digital versions of items and new pathways between these, with the goals of supporting reflection on the structure of items, the relationships between archives and their item sets. Researchers sought to foster engaged reinterpretation of the records of hotel and restaurant workers across multiple archives in British Columbia.

Crossing Fonds created an expanded environment where collections held by counter-archives can, through linked data, occupy a shared archival space, challenge dominant narratives, unite collections shared across multiple archival institutions, or inform contemporary collections seeking to redress inequities in past archival collecting practices. This methodology echoes the still relevant concerns and strategies provided by Kessler-Harris and Rowbotham over four decades ago. The Case Study 1 item sets supported by the Thematic Guide and the Oral History Research support researchers to navigate newly-related documents and provide a coherent aggregation of case study items to allow public engagement with historical documents. Case Study 1 supports an ongoing reappraisal of the history of women workers and unionists, one that builds on research from earlier decades that relied on dispersed physical records, many of which are now digitized and uploaded and aggregated on the platform and are significantly augmented by records from personal archives, a far broader span of union minutes, and genealogical and demographic data. It provided continuity with WLHP transmediated feminist approaches to emerge women’s agency from the historical record.

As much as Case Study 1 is a history of labour union activity, issues, strategies, and actors within these unions, it can equally be used for contemporary archival digital humanities research. Critical archival studies foreground the importance of provenance, collection description, and redescription, creating continuity with second wave feminist critiques of archives and strengthened awareness of marginalized communities, representation, and self-representation, as well as Indigenous data sovereignty. The case study supports an examination of the ways that restaurant workers exert a presence within archives (government, academic, personal, and community-based). What collections are contained there, who were the collectors, who described the fonds, and what networks exist between collections that can inform the subject? The Crossing Fonds platform suggests the value of a curated research space, capable of supporting depth and breadth of analysis.
